title: Perihelion lit notes: long-streams, cost models, and small experiments
content:
Quick framing / motivation:
- Trying to synthesize top takeaways from papers + talks I flagged at NeurIPS/virtual sessions (late Oct->early Nov). Goal: 3 small, cheap experiments we can run on dedicated infra in <2 weeks to validate cost tradeoffs for long-stream customers.

Highlights and very short summaries (my read, biased):
1) Temporal Prompting for Long Streams (paper + workshop talk)
   - Idea: treat long-session drift as a slowly changing latent and use a lightweight updater that stores compressed deltas (not raw tokens).
   - Why it matters: KV cache + recurrent updates are expensive at scale; this reduces per-token attention overhead by ~15-30% in authors' sim.
   - My note: sounds like a cheap prefix-compression layer. Questions: how stable are deltas across sessions? what is quality drop on retrieval-heavy prompts?

2) Sparse+Local Attention Revisited (conference spotlight)
   - New scheduling that interleaves global sparse heads with dense local windows; less brittle than pure sparse patterns for varying sequence lengths.
   - Benchmarks: improved perplexity at high lengths vs block-sparse baselines, with modest compute savings.
   - My note: possibly complementary to our kernel-selection heuristics. Worth adding as a candidate kernel profile in the runtime selector.

3) Practical Edge Cost Modeling (industry talk + blog)
   - Simple param model: unit_cost = fixed_inference_overhead + per_token_compute * tokens + memory-transfer_penalty * top_k_fetches.
   - Emphasis: network/serialization latencies dominate small-batch runs. Authors use 95th-percentile tail to size buffers.
   - My note: aligns with customer reports about 'burstyness' driving costs. We should experiment with small-batch shaping and prefetch heuristics in Dedicated pools.

4) Tiny-kernel fusion for low-bit kernels (poster)
   - Empirical trickset: fuse quant dequant + matmul into one kernel for 4-bit paths; reduces memory traffic and improves throughput on A100-like hardware.
   - My note: may conflict with some of our compile-time assumptions but big win for heavily quantized models. Explore with Miguel's team.

Brainstormed experiments (prioritized):
A) Prefix-delta probe (cheap compression experiment) - 3 days dev, 2x small runs
   - Setup: take 1000 customer-like sessions (anonymized/synth) with ~8k avg tokens. Compute deltas via product quant or PCA on token embeddings every 512 tokens -> store compressed delta + checkpoint.
   - Compare: baseline (full KV cache) vs compressed-delta rehydration. Metrics: token latency, GPU memory, char-level L2 on cached representations, simple QA accuracy on a held prompt set.
   - Win criteria: >10% GPU mem reduction at <2% QA drop and latency within 1.2x baseline.

B) Small-batch shaping + prefetch (cost tail reduction) - 1 week dev + run
   - Setup: instrument dedicated pool to implement a lightweight batch-shaper that delays tiny requests (<=8 tokens) for up to X ms to coalesce; prefetch likely continuation KV for active session ids if idle spike predicted.
   - Compare: tail latency (p50/p95/p99), request compute cost, and effective per-token cost billed (simulate current pricing).
   - Notes: need SRE signoff for traffic shaping behavior.

C) Kernel-profile candidate: sparse-local head schedule (integration with runtime selector) - 2 weeks
   - Setup: add an alternate kernel plan that uses local windows + 2 global sparse heads. Run microbenchmarks on sequence lengths 512, 2048, 8192.
   - Metrics: throughput, tokens/sec, peruplexity proxy on small eval set.

Risks / unknowns / open questions:
- Data sensitivity: cannot sample real customer sessions without privacy/legal review. Use synthetics but ensure distribution matches (token entropy, retrieval patterns).
- Integration complexity for kernel fusion: some models in our catalog rely on fused ops for correctness; need a test harness.
- Customer UX: shaping delays might frustrate interactive apps; propose opt-in per-route shaping with a visible flag in Console.

Notes-to-self / todo list:
- [ ] Draft short experiment brief for prefix-delta probe (include in weeklies, ask for 2 GPUs on dedicated pool).
- [ ] Slack Maya + Owen: can you look at the small-kernel fusion notes and say if we already have partial work? (tag Miguel).
- [ ] Write a quick eval harness that measures QA drop for compressed-delta vs baseline (use internal SQuAD-like set).
- [ ] Check with Legal about sampling anonymized sessions (email privacy@redwood).

Snippets & quick sketches:
- Cheap delta idea: for each 512-token chunk compute mean embedding mu and top-4 PCA components; store mu + coefficients (4 floats) per chunk. Reconstruct during rehydration by adding to base prefix embedding.
- Prefetch heuristic: if session active and last request < 2s, prefetch next likely KV chunk when GPU free for low-priority. Could be gated by route-level budget.

References / links I flagged while reading:
- Temporal Prompting for Long Streams (paper): https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12345 (see section 4 for delta representation)
- Sparse+Local attention demo code: https://github.com/example/sparse-local-demo
- Practical Edge Cost blog: https://engineering.example.com/edge-costs
- Tiny-kernel fusion poster slides (NeurIPS workshop): https://slideshare.example.com/tiny-kernel-fusion

One-paragraph summary for Slack: 
"NeurIPS takeaways: several practical approaches that reduce long-session inference cost — compressed-session deltas, local+sparse attention schedules, and kernel fusion for quant paths. I propose three short probes (prefix-delta, batch-shaping, runtime kernel profile) to get signals on quality vs unit-cost quickly. Draft brief incoming; ping me if you want to join the experiment sprint."

Random musings (late-night):
- Could we expose a 'session-cost' API in the Console: estimated dollars-per-active-session per 1-hour window given route settings? Would help sales and SRE.
- If delta-recons prove stable, we can store compressed checkpoints at route-level and reduce cross-tenant duplication.

End of page.

-- rachel
